metadata.Syllabus Name: Big Data Technologies & Tools_Công cụ và kỹ thuật trên dữ liệu lớn.
metadata.Learning-Teaching Method: Inquiry-Based Learning, In-class lecture, Active Learning
metadata.Time Allocation: Study hour (150h) = 45h contact hours (60 sessions x 45') + 1h final exam + 104h self-study
metadata.Description: This course introduces students to the principles and trade-offs in designing data-intensive systems, using Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd Edition) as the primary textbook.Students will study:1. Trade-offs in data systems architecture: OLTP vs OLAP, Cloud vs Self-Hosting, Distributed vs Single-Node systems.2. Nonfunctional requirements: Scalability, Reliability, and Maintainability.3. Data models: Relational, Document, and Graph-Like models.4. Storage and retrieval: LSM-tree, B-Trees, columnar storage, Cloud Data Warehouses.5. Batch processing: MapReduce and Apache Spark on large-scale public datasets.6. Stream processing: Change Data Capture (CDC), Kafka/Redpanda, log-based messaging.7. Data encoding: JSON, Protocol Buffers, Avro, schema evolution.8. Distributed systems: Replication, Sharding, Transactions, and Isolation.9. End-to-end data pipeline design from OLTP ingestion to OLAP analytical output.
metadata.StudentTasks: - Students must attend at least 80% of contact slots in order to be accepted to the final examination.- Student is responsible to do all exercises, assignments and labs given by instructor in class or at home and submit on time- Use laptop in class only for learning purpose- Promptly access to the FU FLM at https://flm.fpt.edu.vn/ for up-to-date course information

sections.heading: 5 LO(s)
rows: Analyze trade-offs and nonfunctional requirements of data systems, including OLTP versus OLAP, scalability, reliability, and maintainability.
Compare data models, storage engines, and encoding formats to select appropriate solutions for given workloads.
Explain replication, sharding, and transaction isolation in distributed data systems.
Apply batch processing techniques to analyze large datasets using Apache Spark and Spark SQL.
Build streaming data pipelines and design end-to-end systems from OLTP to OLAP.

sections.heading: 10 Constructive question(s)
rows: Why do you think modern companies choose to separate their transaction processing systems (OLTP) from their analytics systems (OLAP), even though this adds complexity?
How would you explain to a non-technical manager why a system that works perfectly with 100 users might fail with 1 million users — and what would you do about it?
Why might choosing a document database over a relational database for a social network make the application faster to build but harder to maintain over time?
Why do you think column-oriented storage is better suited for analytics queries than row-oriented storage, even though both contain the same data?
Why is it important that a new version of an application can still read data written by an older version — and what happens when this backward compatibility breaks?
How can two simultaneous bank transfers from the same distributed account both succeed and leave it overdrawn — and what database mechanism prevents this?
Why might processing the same dataset take minutes with MapReduce but seconds with Spark — and when would you still choose MapReduce over Spark?
How would you explain why running the same Spark SQL query on CSV versus Parquet produces identical results but very different performance — and what does this tell you about columnar storage?
How does Change Data Capture (CDC) allow analytics systems to stay up-to-date without putting load on the production database?
Looking at the CDC pipeline you built in Lab 05 (PostgreSQL to Redpanda to MinIO to ClickHouse), at which point does data transform from a transactional record into an analytical insight?
